    def construct(self):
        # Setup Layout
        title = "The Translation Problem"
        lines = [
            "How do we translate Pixel's coordinates to ours?",
            "We follow his tilted arrows on our standard grid.",
            "This calculation bridges the two different perspectives."
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title, lines)

        # Colors
        V1_COLOR = "#FFFF00"  # Yellow (Basis vector 1)
        V2_COLOR = "#00FFFF"  # Cyan (Basis vector 2)
        VECTOR_COLOR = "#FFFFFF" # White (Pixel's vector)
        RESULT_COLOR = "#00FF00" # Green (Standard coordinates result)
        SKEWED_GRID_COLOR = "#555555" # Dimmed skewed grid
        STD_GRID_COLOR = "#333333" # Dimmed standard grid

        # Basis vectors defined in Section 3
        v1 = np.array([2, 1, 0])
        v2 = np.array([-1, 1, 0])
        
        # 1. Coordinate System Mobjects
        # Standard Grid
        std_grid = NumberPlane(
            x_range=[-1, 5, 1],
            y_range=[-1, 5, 1],
            background_line_style={"stroke_color": STD_GRID_COLOR, "stroke_opacity": 0.5}
        ).set_z_index(-1)
        
        # Skewed Grid (Pixel's basis)
        skewed_grid = NumberPlane(
            x_range=[-1, 2.5, 1],
            y_range=[-1, 2.5, 1],
            background_line_style={"stroke_color": SKEWED_GRID_COLOR, "stroke_opacity": 0.8}
        )
        # Columns of matrix are the basis vectors v1 and v2
        matrix = [[2, -1], [1, 1]]
        skewed_grid.apply_matrix(matrix)
        
        # Main Vector in Pixel's basis: [2, 1]_B
        # This maps to 2*v1 + 1*v2 = [3, 3] in standard coordinates
        pixel_point = 2 * v1 + 1 * v2
        main_vector = Arrow(ORIGIN, pixel_point, buff=0, color=VECTOR_COLOR)
        label_b = MathTex(r"[2, 1]_B", color=VECTOR_COLOR).scale(0.8)
        label_b.next_to(main_vector.get_end(), UR, buff=0.1)
        
        # Chained vectors for visual addition: 2*v1 then 1*v2
        arrow_v1_1 = Arrow(ORIGIN, v1, buff=0, color=V1_COLOR, stroke_width=4)
        arrow_v1_2 = Arrow(v1, 2*v1, buff=0, color=V1_COLOR, stroke_width=4)
        arrow_v2_add = Arrow(2*v1, 2*v1 + v2, buff=0, color=V2_COLOR, stroke_width=4)
        path_arrows = VGroup(arrow_v1_1, arrow_v1_2, arrow_v2_add)
        
        label_2v1 = MathTex("2 \\cdot v_1", color=V1_COLOR).scale(0.7)

        label_std.next_to(res_point, RIGHT, buff=0.2)
        
        # Positioning Logic
        # Focus on the area where the transformation occurs (approx origin to (4,3))
        focus_center = np.array([1.5, 1.5, 0])
        all_visuals = VGroup(
            std_grid, skewed_grid, main_vector, label_b, 
            path_arrows, label_2v1, label_v2, res_point, label_std
        )
        all_visuals.shift(-focus_center)
        # Resolved issues 41, 42, 43 by adjusting area to B2:F6 and scale to 0.4

        # Initially hide components for progressive reveal

        path_arrows.set_opacity(0)
        label_2v1.set_opacity(0)
        label_v2.set_opacity(0)
        res_point.set_opacity(0)

outline.topic: Change of Basis: Seeing the World Through Different Perspectives

sections.title: The Concept of Perspective
sections.content: Introduce the idea that the same physical point in space can be described by different sets of coordinates depending on the observer's orientation. Use a character to ground the concept.
sections.example: Character 'Pixel the Robot' is standing in a room. From our perspective (Standard Basis), Pixel is at (3, 2). But from Pixel's own tilted perspective, he might feel like he is just 2 units forward and 1 unit left. The point is the same; the labels are different.

sections.title: Prerequisite Check: The Standard Basis
sections.content: Briefly review how we usually describe vectors as linear combinations of the standard unit vectors i (1,0) and j (0,1). Use a standard square grid visual.
sections.example: Visualizing the vector [3, 2] as 3 steps along the x-axis and 2 steps along the y-axis. These axes are our 'language' for space.

sections.title: Defining a New Basis
sections.content: Introduce a new set of basis vectors, B = {v1, v2}. Explain that for these to be a basis, they must be linearly independent (not pointing in the same line). Transform the square grid into a tilted/stretched grid.
sections.example: Let v1 = [2, 1] and v2 = [-1, 1]. In our world, these are arrows. In 'Pixel's World', these are his new unit steps. Animation shows the standard grid morphing into this new slanted coordinate system.

sections.title: The Translation Problem
sections.content: Explain the core goal: How do we translate 'Pixel's coordinates' into 'Our coordinates'? Introduce the notation [x]B for coordinates in the new basis and x for standard coordinates.
sections.example: If Pixel says he is at [2, 1] in his basis, we calculate: 2 * (his v1) + 1 * (his v2). Graphically, we follow his tilted arrows to find the final landing spot on our grid.

sections.title: The Change of Basis Matrix (P)
sections.content: Show that the translation process is just matrix multiplication. The 'Change of Basis Matrix' P is formed by placing the new basis vectors into the columns of a matrix.
sections.example: Matrix P = [[2, -1], [1, 1]]. If Pixel's coordinate is [2, 1], we multiply P * [2, 1]^T to get [3, 3]^T in our standard system. Animation highlights the columns of P being the basis vectors.

sections.title: The Reverse Journey (P-Inverse)
sections.content: Explain how to go from our world back to Pixel's world using the inverse matrix. This is crucial for understanding how different systems communicate.
sections.example: If we want to tell Pixel where a point (5, 4) is in his language, we use the inverse of P. Calculation: [x]B = P⁻¹ * x. Visual shows 'undoing' the tilt of the grid to return to a standard square view.

sections.title: Summary and Real-world Application
sections.content: Summarize that Change of Basis is just a 'dictionary' between two languages of space. Mention why we do this: some problems are easier to solve in a specific basis (like Eigenvectors or image compression).
sections.example: Mention JPEG compression: It changes the basis of image pixels into a 'frequency basis' where it's easier to throw away unimportant data without us noticing.
